title: The OSI & TCP/IP Models: How Network Layers Stack
oneLiner: Every network request is really several layers wrapping each other's output -- each one only has to understand its own layer, not the whole stack.
keyTakeaway: Data goes DOWN the stack on the sender (each layer wraps the previous layer's output in its own header -- encapsulation) and back UP the stack on the receiver (each layer strips its own header off -- decapsulation). The 7-layer OSI model is the textbook reference; the 4-layer TCP/IP model is what real stacks (and tools like Wireshark) actually implement -- OSI's Application/Presentation/Session collapse into one TCP/IP Application layer, and Physical/Data Link collapse into one Link layer.
explanation:
"Layers" here means each piece of the stack only has to understand its OWN job and talk to its direct counterpart on the other end -- the Transport layer on your laptop doesn't know or care whether the Wi-Fi or the Ethernet cable underneath it is doing the actual carrying, and the Application layer doesn't know or care whether TCP is retransmitting a lost segment underneath it. That separation is the same idea as this app's own IConcept/ITool interfaces (see Interfaces & Abstraction on the roadmap) -- program to a boundary, not the details behind it. OSI's 7-layer version is the textbook teaching model; real network stacks (and what a packet-capture tool like Wireshark actually shows you) implement the simpler 4-layer TCP/IP model instead, which folds OSI's top three layers into one "Application" layer and its bottom two into one "Link" layer.

A protocol is an agreed set of rules for a conversation between machines, and each layer has its own; HTTP is the protocol browsers and web servers use. Walk one HTTP request down and back up to see why the layering matters: your browser (Application) builds an HTTP request and hands it down. TCP (Transport) wraps it in a segment, adding a header (a small block of addressing and control information) with the port numbers that say which PROGRAM on each machine this is for. IP (Internet) wraps that in a packet, adding the source/destination IP addresses that say which MACHINE it's for (see IP Addressing & Subnetting for how an address itself is structured). Ethernet or Wi-Fi (Link) wraps that in a frame, adding the MAC addresses (the hardware addresses built into each network card) for the physical hop to the next device, then the Physical layer turns it into an actual electrical, radio, or light signal on the wire or over the air. The receiving machine does every one of those steps in reverse, one layer unwrapping the next, until the original HTTP request lands back at an application layer on the other end.
